judge_assessment.explanation: Everything the judge recomputed, I recomputed and confirm: slope (90−62)/(50−10) = 0.7; b = 62 − 0.7·10 = 55 giving y = 0.7x + 55; the prediction 0.7·60 + 55 = 97; the negative fit (5−9)/(8−0) = −0.5 with y = −0.5x + 9; the prediction −0.5·7 + 9 = 5.5 against the plotted 5.7, a gap of 0.2; the shoe-size mean 612/8 = 76.5; the plant ranges 40−3 = 37 and 15−3 = 12; and the absurd extrapolation 0.7·200 + 55 = 195 against a 100-point quiz. I also verified the claim the judge only gestures at — that the plots support the keyed readings. They do exactly: worksheet.tex line 34 plots (10,62)…(55,93), byte-for-byte the data array in verify.json id 1, and every one of the twelve figures reuses one of the four arrays with no drift. Where I go further than the judge: three printed responses are neither machine-checked nor flagged manual. Problem 5 asks the student to 'say whether this is an interpolation or an extrapolation' and id 5 holds only the eval for 97. Problem 9 asks 'Which is larger, and by how much?' — the key answers 0.2 of an hour, and 0.2 is never an expected; only the two endpoints 5.5 and 5.7 are checked. Problem 11 says 'Name the outlier' and id 11 checks the two ranges only, so the point (8,40) that the whole problem is about is unverified. Problem 3 additionally instructs 'Draw a line of fit on the plot below' — a marked representation with no manual entry, though the author cleverly pinned the line through two named points so the slope itself stays checkable. None of this touches the ACCEPT, and the judge's six manual items really are correctly flagged with model answers.

strengths_to_preserve: Problem 3 pins the line of fit through (10,62) and (50,90) so that a by-eye construction produces a determinate, machine-checkable slope. That is the right way to make an inherently informal skill verifiable without faking it — keep this pattern for any 'draw a line and read from it' item.

The four data sets carry distinct pedagogical jobs and the sheet uses each twice: revision/score (positive), screen time/sleep (negative), shoe size/score (genuinely no association, so problem 10 is the item where the correct answer is 'do not draw a line'), and the plant heights whose eighth point (8,40) breaks a 2-cm-a-day pattern.

Problem 12 closes on 195 points out of a 100-point quiz and asks why nobody should trust it. Making the extrapolation arithmetically correct and obviously impossible is a better teacher than any warning box.

Every problem carries its own copy of its scatter plot, so no page has to be flipped back to — and the twelve copies are all generated from the same four coordinate lists, so the pictures cannot disagree with the checks.

root_causes.description: Coverage is granted per problem id, so an id whose principal numeric answer is checked can carry additional printed asks — a classification, a difference, a named point — that no entry pins down. All three are machine-checkable; none was machine-checked.
evidence: Problem 5 stem: 'say whether this is an interpolation or an extrapolation'; verify.json id 5 = one eval, expected 97.
Problem 9 stem: 'Which is larger, and by how much?'; id 9 = eval 5.5 and read_data 5.7 — the answer 0.2 that the key prints is not an expected.
Problem 11 stem: 'Name the outlier'; id 11 = two stats/range entries, expected 37 and 12 — the point (8,40) is never checked.
gate_log.txt: 12 boxed answers against 12 problem segments, all gates green — the binding gate counts boxed answers per problem, not asks per problem.

root_causes.description: A drawn or marked response has no representation in the verification record at all. Problem 3 requires a line drawn on a printed plot; the JSON can express the slope of that line but not the fact that a human must look at the drawing.
evidence: Problem 3 stem: 'Draw a line of fit on the plot below: a straight line that passes as close as possible to as many points as possible, with roughly as many points above it as below it.'

The answer key's solution for 3 teaches the drawing rules ('it does not have to touch any point') but prints no acceptance criteria for the drawn line, unlike the six ids that do carry manual entries.

improvements.title: Check the classification, the difference and the named point that problems 5, 9 and 11 ask for
improvements.proposed_change: Add the missing expecteds: a string/compare entry on id 5 recording 'extrapolation', an eval entry on id 9 for 5.7 − 5.5 = 0.2, and a read_data max_key (or explicit point) entry on id 11 naming (8,40). More generally, make the coverage gate count the distinct quantities a stem asks for — the stems here enumerate them with 'and' and question marks — and fail when a problem's entries supply fewer expecteds than the stem requests, so an unchecked sub-answer cannot ride along on a checked one.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture: a problem whose stem reads 'Predict … Then read the actual value … Which is larger, and by how much?' with a verify.json id holding only the two endpoint entries. The coverage gate must fail naming the uncovered difference; adding the eval entry must make it pass. Today this shape builds green (curr-247's gate_log.txt).
improvements.expected_impact: The residual 0.2, the interpolation/extrapolation call and the outlier's identity move from 'stated in the key' to 'proved before printing', and each appears in the Quick Answers bank where a grader can use it.
improvements.risk: Parsing 'how many answers does this stem ask for' from prose is heuristic and will misfire on rhetorical questions; pair it with an author-declared ask count so a false positive can be resolved deliberately rather than by weakening the gate.

improvements.title: Declare problem 3's drawn line of fit as a manual item alongside its checkable slope
improvements.proposed_change: Where a stem instructs the student to draw, plot, mark, shade or sketch, require a manual entry on that id carrying the acceptance criteria the grader should apply — for problem 3: a single straight line, roughly equal numbers of points above and below, not the line joining the first and last dots, passing through the two named points. Keep the slope check as well: the item is then correctly recorded as part machine-verified, part read by hand, which is what it is.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture worksheet whose problem stem begins 'Draw a line of fit …' with a verify.json id holding only a slope entry. The gate must exit non-zero naming the drawing; adding a manual entry must make it pass.
improvements.expected_impact: Every response a computer cannot see — the mark on the page — is handed to the human with criteria, and the sheet's manual count (6 today) becomes an accurate description of what a teacher must actually read.
improvements.risk: Low, but it will add manual entries to every graphing-heavy sheet; the report must distinguish 'manual because drawn' from 'manual because open reasoning' so a reader does not conclude the mathematics went unchecked.

case_summary: The strongest packet in this batch. Twelve problems, each with its own plot generated from one of four coordinate lists that match verify.json exactly; a difficulty walk that runs read a point → describe → draw a fit → write its equation → predict → and then two items where the right answer is that no line should be drawn or that the prediction is worthless; and a key that shows the substitution before every prediction. Six open items are correctly flagged manual with model answers, and final_response.md names all three PDFs by filename. The gaps are narrow and all of one kind: three printed sub-answers (the interpolation/extrapolation call in 5, the 0.2 difference in 9, the named outlier in 11) are machine-checkable but unchecked, and problem 3's drawn line has no manual entry. The judge's page criticism is soft — the build's own budget calls for nine pages and the sheet used seven — so I would not have deducted there.
